quotes.excerpt: The Big Shakedown #1 is a confident debut that pairs imaginative post-disaster worldbuilding with a compelling lead and a strong central mystery. Jordan Blum and Tim Seeley establish a fractured California that feels dangerous, satirical, and lived in, while Scott Koblish and Hi-Fi give the setting vivid visual character. With Ester’s personal goals tied directly to the missing-person case, the issue delivers an engaging start and plenty of reasons to return. This should be a strong contender when deciding what to pick up at the shop this week. Trust me once you read this first issue you will definitely want to add this series to your Pull List.

The Big Shakedown‘s premiere issue is a gritty post-natural disaster mystery with more unanswered questions and mystery than those answered. Tim Seeley. Jordan Blum, and Scott Koblish deliver a fresh tale with an edge and mystery that pulls you into a dark and frightening Los Angeles that is even hard for the reader to escape. The Big Shakedown is a vivid, character-driven mystery that turns a shattered Los Angeles into an intriguing and frightening noir setting.

The things that Haun and his team are doing are truly electric and terrifying. “Dooney Hollow” is for those that love slow burn horror with plenty of mystery and fall vibes. If you want that, then you need to pick this up!

The Folk of Dooney Hollow #1 is a compelling horror debut that pairs a steadily unfolding mystery with atmospheric artwork and an unsettling Ozark setting. Its strong pacing, memorable final reveal, and lingering unanswered questions make the next issue an easy recommendation. Make sure to pick a copy of this first issue up when you are at the shop this week. Also, well you are there, you should just add this to your Pull List as I’m confident that you will want more of this amazing and eerie world.

Conan the Barbarian #35 is another winning issue in a winning arc. Jim Zub’s tale of Conan and his allies confronting a cosmic horror ranks up there with the best of Robert E. Howard’s stories, and the art is a gorgeous fit for the material.

The Brutal Dark is poised to strike but Ezra Cain is flying into the heart of danger in this exciting chapter. Condon wraps up events  with a direct shot of intensity. Phillips’ art takes readers on a roller-coaster ride of emotions.  A great “so long for now”, but definitely not “goodbye forever”.
While the finale feels a little abrupt, Peril of the Brutal Dark: An Ezra Cain Mystery #6 is still a great final issue for one of the best series of the year.
Power Rangers Unlimited #1 is a bold, legacy embracing start which easily grabs hold of the best of BOOM!-era Power Rangers comics and presents it from a fresh and exciting angle.

Power Rangers Unlimited #1 delivers an action-packed debut that leans into Power Rangers history from a fresh point of view, and when combined with the out-of-this-world art and extensive roster, Power Rangers Unlimited becomes a must-read for any and every fan of the franchise.

After a long, strange journey, 'Is Ted OK?' concludes with a massively satisfying final issue, showcasing the book's identity, intent, and innovation that has made this book one of 2026's biggest standouts.

Is Ted OK? #6 sticks the landing and brings an amazing ending to this unique and awesome series. The uniqueness of the story brings readers in, but the drama and emotions are what really keep readers hooked. The ending is fitting and conclusive but does leave the door open to return to this world as well. I for one would welcome another chapter of this amazing story. If you are like me and have been reading this series issue by issue, you will be very happy with this conclusion to the story. However, if you sat this one out, I’ve got great options for you, get to your local shop and hope they have all 6 issues, wait for the Trade Paperback and enjoy, or head over to Neon Ichiban and get every issue NOW! No matter what you ultimately choose, one thing is for sure you need to read this series in its entirety.

John Romita Senior based her appearance on that of Hollywood star Ann Margret. She’s evolved a lot ove the years through numerous different interpretations across a few different formats. She remains an enduring figure who just hasn’t quite gotten the right exposure necessary to really catapult her into her own title successfully. Hopefully Allen and Noto are able to find that illusive formula that’s going to fully allow her to meet her potential on the comic book page. She’s been quite a survivor over the years. Given the right dynamic, she could really shine.

This was a really great trip down memory lane. It’s a great quick retrospective of MJ, and how, love it or hate it, she is intrinsically tied to Peter Parker/Spider-Man. Yet, the authors and artists still show us that MJ is her own person with her own dreams, hopes, and fears.

White Boat #3 brings the series to a close with confidence, tying together its themes of guilt, control, and the unknown in a way that feels both unsettling and satisfying. Scott Snyder keeps the emotional core centered on Lee, giving his journey a sense of purpose even as the world around him spirals into chaos. The reveal of the island’s true nature adds weight to the story’s central ideas, while the final act pushes the horror into overdrive. Francesco Francavilla’s art elevates every moment, making the danger feel immediate and the environment oppressive. It is a finale that sticks with you, even as it leaves some of its mysteries lingering.

White Boat #3 is a fitting end to a wild story. The twist and turns keep you off the scent of how this story will actually end. However, once we enter the end game the issue picks up in the form of violence and action. The artwork is equally as good and competes with the story for the readers’ attention.
G.I. Joe #25 is a major milestone done right, paying off years of buildup and kicking off the series' most epic storyline yet.

G.I. JOE #25 is a phenomenal start to the Nightforce story arc. Joshua Williamson, Tom Reilly and Andrea Milana pace things out that you feel like you are experiencing the start of a big blockbuster event. Everything that happens in this issue comes across as being a payoff for many sub-plots that have been developed since the start of the series. Where the payoff leads to is anyone’s guess, leaving you as the reader even more excited to find out what happens next.

Superman #40 is damn near perfect. This arc acted as a bit of a redemption for Superboy Prime and I absolutely adore him after this. Whilst the story here is wrapped up, this isn’t the last time we will see Superboy Prime and there seems to be a bright future ahead for him and his “supporting characters”.

This has been a phenomenal story setting up Prime’s future, but special credit once again goes to Dan Mora, who plays with the nature of the comic book format in some incredibly unique ways. The original Superman is back next month for the kickoff of the big “Kingdom of Zod” event, but I hope Williamson gets to keep writing Prime for a long time.

Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #300 (#20) not only pushes the great story that we have been following forward, but also gives this milestone issue a big feel as well. The drama, action, surprises, and emotions are firing on all cylinders in this issue. If this issue doesn’t make you feel something you may need to check your pulse. They could’ve just phoned this one in as the 300th issue milestone is more than enough to sell the book. But they didn’t phone it in at all and crafted an issue that is sure to bring readers back next month for issue 21. If Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles is not on your Pull List already it needs to be added ASAP! If you are a comic book collector this 300th issue needs to be added to your collection as well. Cheers to 300 issues of TMNT and can’t wait for the 400th milestone issue!

This issue takes you on an emotional ride! Sure there is plenty of action within these pages. All while tugging at your heart strings with the current situation revolving around Shen. Losing a loved one and having the chance to bring them back is going to hit home with many readers I suspect. You do not want to miss out on this start of a new storyline for this series of TMNT. Go get your copy today!
Power Rangers Unlimited #1 is a bold, legacy embracing start which easily grabs hold of the best of BOOM!-era Power Rangers comics and presents it from a fresh and exciting angle.

Power Rangers Unlimited #1 delivers an action-packed debut that leans into Power Rangers history from a fresh point of view, and when combined with the out-of-this-world art and extensive roster, Power Rangers Unlimited becomes a must-read for any and every fan of the franchise.

Operation: Iron Coffin #2 keeps the momentum going with a bigger, bloodier, and more personal chapter for Dracula. Kenny Porter deepens the story without slowing down the action, while Tyrell Cannon’s artwork delivers the chaos, horror, and energy this concept demands. This series continues to be an absolute blast and remains an easy Pull List recommendation. Do not sleep on this series! Make sure you jump on this train now, as you don’t want to miss what happens next.

I don’t know how they’re doing it, but “Operation: Iron Coffin” is one of the best out this year. Kenny Porter manages to create a version of Dracula that feels relatable yet horrifying. His writing coupled with Cannon’s fantastic artwork create a truly amazing reading experience.
One of the best series in comics right now. The art is wild, creative, adventurous, and stunning. The story keeps drawing you back in issue after issue.
Marc Spector: Moon Knight #7 delivers an exhilarating ride with huge action, incredible artwork, and deadly stakes. It leaves you itching for the next issue.

The Smart Division is a fantastic science-fiction mystery that eerily could be more fact than fiction. Writer Zack Kaplan delivers a timely detective tale exploring the use of modern technology in solving crimes. However, it’s the juxtaposition of John Pearson’s elegant brush strokes that makes story rise above the rest. Kaplan and Pearson’s creativity knows no bounds and The Smart Division is proof of that.

I sat down with The Smart Division expecting a slick sci-fi detective story and walked away rattled about the world outside my window. That is the highest thing I can say about a comic right now. This is a perfect debut and one of the most relevant books on the stands, and I cannot wait to see where the case goes.

King Shazam and Superman throw down in a final fight for the ages! Arron leaves it all on table with the script. The art team never knows a ceiling in how far to raise the stakes. Highest possible recommendation.

Absolute Superman #21 feels like a true spectacle and lives up to the hype in every way as this arc comes to. a close. There is so much violence, emotion, and power packed into these pages that it may, in fact, be my favorite issue of the run yet.

Operation: Iron Coffin comes out of the gate swinging with a unique premise that delivers far more than ever expected. Kenny Porter and Tyrell Cannon give us a Dracula that isn’t just here for the carnage, although we get plenty of that, but for a compelling redemption arc wrapped in a fast-paced, blood-soaked WWII setting. IDW Dark may have some heavy hitting titles in its first year as an imprint at IDW Publishing, but Operation: Iron Coffin stands out as one of the best.

Operation Coffin #1 is a stylish debut for Porter and Cannon’s new take on Dracula. A truly unique premise, backed by engaging lore and a curious mission have already laid the groundwork for a wild ride ahead.
Superman: The Stranger #1 returns to Clark Kent's roots, spinning a story that shows why Superman is such a timeless character.

The best Superman comic I’ve read in years!  A 1930s reinvention of the Man of Steel that returns Superman to his 1930s roots, but zigs and zags in ways you won’t expect, while keeping you on your toes. With a story that hooks you from the go and art and colours that leap off the page, this is a must-read mini-series.

Six of Us #1 turns a seemingly perfect 1990s sitcom cast into a web of secrets, resentment, and murder, with Tom King and Gabriel Hernández Walta delivering a compelling mystery that leaves everyone looking potentially guilty.

SIX OF US reminds us why this award winning creative team is so unstoppable. It's a human story about the importance of creating art, but the cost of it too. Six of Us #1 invites us to consider what true fulfillment looks like, and whether it has anything to do with success.
Black Tower: The Raven Conspiracy #1 is a compelling mix of magic and spy fiction, packed with haunting imagery and a unique mystery.

Black Tower: The Raven Conspiracy #1 proves that everything out of DC Vertigo should be jumped on immediately. This was a strong start to a comic series that has captured my attention from the first page and didn’t let go until the ending. I cannot recommend this comic enough!

This was SUCH a good ending to this arc. How everything ended, how the characters handled the situations, and the pure emotions that ran throughout this issue, everything was beautifully handled. Gail Simone, Luciano Vecchio, Matthew Wilson, and Clayton Cowles should be very proud of themselves for this one.

The X-Men battle pure evil on two fronts in an exciting arc finale! Simone unleashes the fury behind heroic eyes with a fantastic script. Vecchio and Wilson craft intense images that never let up on the magnitude of the events. This run of UXM what you set the benchmark for modern X-Men stories to hit!

Poison Ivy #48 stands out as a beautifully crafted and deeply immersive experience. G. Willow Wilson’s writing, combined with the perfectly suited art style and accessible lettering, makes for a compelling read that leaves a lasting impression of hope despite the high stakes.

Isley’s visions of grandeur crash all around her as reality of politics sinks in. Wilson exposes the frail state of affairs with solid writing. Takara & Prianto craft the sinking looks of hope with each emotional panel. With nothing left, Isely now embarks on a more dangerous journey: rebuilding from nothing left.
X-Men #38 serves as a deep character piece for Magneto, reaffirming the Master of Magnetism's place with the X-Men and in the world.

A solid issue that provides readers with some of the most compelling dialogue of the year. Jed MacKay’s work is must read material that you can’t pass up on. Together with artwork that is stupendous, this is an issue you can’t wait on reading!

If I hadn’t known this was a “Giant Sized” issue, or seen the number of pages, I would have never known. I was so quickly caught up in the story and the captivating art that I was completely unaware of how many pages I had read. Geiger #25 absolutely killed it with the story, the emotion, the art, and setting up what’s looking to be a very exciting future… and past. I truly can’t say enough amazing things about this comic. Each issue creates a new pathway for our Glowing Man. Some inspiring, some tragic, but always entertaining.

Geiger #25 delivers a powerful payoff to the battle with Griffin, combining explosive action, emotional consequences, and outstanding visuals. The issue also pushes the larger Unnamed Universe forward with intriguing new possibilities. As both a conclusion and a launch point for what comes next, this is another excellent issue in Ghost Machine’s flagship series. This is a must grab issue at the shop this week and a worthwhile add to your Pull List as you won’t want to miss where this story is going.

I really enjoyed the way this story was able to simultaneously tie into the DNX event while still feeling like a Fantastic Four story. I’m always a little leery of tie-ins, but this creative team showed that they are up to the task.

Fantastic Four #17 ties into DNX, yet stands on its own two feet with a mystery that reminds readers what's kept this team intact for years. And given where the First Family is located, teamwork is essential to surviving.

The Rocketfellers have never forgotten what their one true goal has been, and always will be: protecting their kids. Despite this issue being a fantastic story introducing more mystery and new faces, it’s still authentic. Mom still worries and puts her kids above everything. I truly love that about this comic. It makes this time-traveling, monsters, aliens, demons, and angel world feel more grounded and relatable. I’m very excited to see where we go from here, as the Rocketfellers’ world is definitely growing, and based on those last couple of pages it’s about to get even more chaotic.

Though the particulars are substantially different, it's hard to readt The Rocketfellers and not be heavily reminded of the original Fantastic Four.. it's a family of people who went up in a rocket and are embroiled in weird science fiction adventures is kind of their thing. And since they've been so high profile for so long, it's kind of hard to do anything that's even remotely in that same vein without seeming like a week imitation. TOmasi and company have been at it for long enough that their particular family feels distinctive and unique.
I've enjoyed this book since issue one. I'm gonna keep enjoying this book. It’s just a fun easy read of just what you want from a superhero comic.

However, life is about the journey, not the destination, and this issue is no exception. Saladin Ahmed crafts a classic Wolverine adventure that checks all the boxes that a Wolverine fan would have: a flannel-wearing Logan joining forces with another X-Man to slash his way into a bloody battle against an iconic foe. Despite the simple story, issue #28 is not without thematic merit. The comic begins with Forge and Logan chatting it up at a restaurant. Ahmed really understands what makes Wolverine tick as a character in these quieter scenes: his sarcasm, his brashness, and his underlying care for those close to him. The dialogue feels incredibly natural and in-character for both X-Men. At the end of the comic, Wolverine speaks to a character from this volumes’ past; it’s a very simple scene that adds nothing to the overall plot of the comic. Nonetheless, this scene excels because of how human it feels for these characters: a genuine moment of emotional tenderness for Logan in a life of p

Conan the Barbarian #35 is another winning issue in a winning arc. Jim Zub’s tale of Conan and his allies confronting a cosmic horror ranks up there with the best of Robert E. Howard’s stories, and the art is a gorgeous fit for the material.

Feral #26 is a character-driven issue which explores Elsie’s insecurities and self-doubt. By examining the character’s anxieties, the reader is able to see Elsie at her most sympathetic and identifiable. Elsie’s feeling that she is not good enough is an all too common feeling for so many of us, and it’s what makes Elsie so relatable and endearing in this issue.

Nevertheless, it's quite dramatic. And it runs the risk of being a little over the top in places. However, it's not very often that this particular series takes a opportunity to look back. It's been one long chase for survival over the course of much of the series. So it's really nice to get a breather like this back over everything that's happened before. At the same time, it's a look ahead. Fleecs and company take a solid close-up on one of the central characters in the ensemble. Her inner emotions are shown in vivid clarity before the series can progress.

Having too much story to tell in this particular instance is perfectly fine. None of it seems to be dragging at all. It's all genuinely quite interesting. The way the writing team brings it to the art team. The way the art team brings it to the page. It all seems really interesting. But it really seems to be a situation where the plots being rendered would probably be a lot more comfortable under different covers. There are two main stories getting addressed in the issue. Each one of them could have their own title.

The Kingdom has fallen but long live the King? That is the question posed in this latest chapter. Williamson sets the stage for an epic finale. The art team captures the personal toll taken as one more attack looks to bring the house down, ready for not. A crossover event living up to the marque billing.
Superman #42 is less an important issue and more of a stopgap as it builds up the finale of the Kingdom of Zod storyline. Hopefully, that finale is worth the wait.

The Fast Food life has caught up with Kyle Rayner at a most inopportune time. Adams nails the laughs while staging the more serious points. The art teams leave nothign to chance with the action. This is a story that can only be told in the pages of Green Lantern.

Green Lantern #39 is a fun conclusion to this strange little food fight, but the Kyle Rayner/Major Force confrontation is the real meal of the issue. Adams continues to show that Kyle’s history matters, and seeing him confront Major Force with a little more maturity gives their rivalry a fresh dimension. The food comedy may be a bit much at times, but the character work, art, Jade’s continued presence, and setup for “First Light” leave me excited for what comes next.

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: Zatanna #6 is a fast-paced and eventful issue that shows Zatanna’s growth while she tries to save the Hidden City. Jamal Campbell’s compelling writing paired with gorgeous visuals by himself, Andrew Dalhouse and Ariana Maher makes this an issue that was with the wait.
pros: Ariana Maher’s letters make this issue easy and entertaining to read.
Jamal Campbell’s slow building of the world of magic places certain scenes and spells Zatanna uses into context without over explaining.
Campbell’s artwork and they way he uses different panels makes for visually interesting but gorgeous pages
cons: I wish we knew more about Atik’s motives other than he was ignored.

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: The Smart Division #2 is sharp techno-noir, with stylish layouts and an interesting premise. However, the second issue doesn't quite live up to the promise of the first, losing momentum in the issue's closing act.
pros: John J. Pearson's layouts provide a lot of depth to the story, creating interesting visual moments.
Writer Zack Kaplan and letterer Buddy Beaudoin do a great job with the beats of the dialogue.
cons: This issue lacks the urgency of the debut.
The ending here veers a bit too close to the ending of the debut to feel novel.

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: This book continues to be a visual delight, delivering on its body horror/erotic romance premise in spectacular fashion. Gastronomique #2 invites you to read it more than once with its imagery.
pros: Nisha Singh's colors are lush and beautiful.
Helena Masellis' characters are ethereal and grotesque.
Marguerite Bennett and Jodie Troutman do a great job working with the artwork to tell the story.

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: X-Men United #7 helps solidify a classic thematic direction: that the X-Men are here to help the world beyond simply mutant affairs.
pros: The artwork by Ruairí Coleman is great with good expression work and gesture.
Eve L. Ewing and Evan Narcisse do a good job making this story both new-reader friendly and thematically resonant.
cons: The nature of how Graymatter Lane works is still under-defined.
The section with the students near the end of the book feels a little flat, as if it's cutting the momentum of the book.

pros: Keeps the DNX connections light until the very last page, which is a geniune surprise.
Though the Four might have lost their memories, North slowly reminds fans why these characters work as a team.
Carratu's artwork embraces the insanity of the Four's powers.
Delgado's colors add the right amount of mystery and dread to the proceedings.

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: A Quiet Place: Rising Tides #1 understands that the franchise works best when silence complicates an already difficult human situation. Declan Shalvey centers the story on Grace's attempt to reconnect with her estranged father, then turns the alien invasion into another barrier between two people who already struggle to communicate. The boat setting is especially effective, creating an enclosed sp…
pros: Grace and her father's strained relationship gives the survival story emotional weight
Silent sequences make excellent use of the comics medium
The alien imagery is appropriately creepy
cons: A quicker read given the silent scenes

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: X-Men #38 serves as a deep character piece for Magneto, reaffirming the Master of Magnetism's place with the X-Men and in the world.
pros: MacKay reinforces Magneto and Xavier's bond as a core concept of the X-Men.
Daniel delivers both epic X-Men imagery and quiet moments with Magneto in equal measure.
Xavier's presence remains ambiguous, which is a great thing.
Deepens the story of DNX yet also stands on its own.

pros: G. Willow Wilson's writing is well paced, digestible and wholly immersive
Interior art by Marcio Takara is reminiscent of how foliage and plant life twists and flows in the wind; it encapsulates Poison Ivy’s wild, spirited ways so per…
Cover art by Jessica Fong is deadly and delightful (who doesn't love a fierce tailored pant suit?)

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: Surprisingly funny and sweet, The Amazing Venom #1 is a debut issue that, while exposition-heavy, is bolstered by the fun chemistry of its two leads.
pros: Feels like a spiritual successor to Superior Foes of Spider-Man
Jordan Morris' script absolutely nails the dynamic of Fred and Passenger, making you actually care for them
Luke Ross' art is able to use great panel design and dynamic layouts to make even the exposition parts of the book stand out
Legitimately funny throughout, and refreshingly does its own weird thing
cons: Some may feel like the opening pages are bogged down too much in filling in new readers on Comeback
Relies a bit too much on outside events to set up the story

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: The vast cast Christopher Priest has built over the years are all on seemingly separate journeys in Vampirella #6 as each looks for clarity and meaning.
pros: Davis Goetten's character expressions and gesture work are superb, allowing the quieter scenes to really resonate.
Color artist Giovanni Caputo's color work is really shown off this issue with impressive use of lighting.
Christopher Priest's scripting remains great, with a good use of tension.
cons: The scenes here all work, but the book itself feels disjointed. Momentum doesn't build between scenes.

reason.label: AIPT review
reason.snippet: What Burnham, Schoening, Myer and Delgado have done on this series for 40+ issues is nothing short of amazing. So many lifelong TMNT fans were introduced to these characters through the 1987 cartoon and they've absolutely done those fans proud. They consistently delivered the kind of energetic, heartfelt and genuinely funny adventures that made this version of the Turtles so memorable in the first…
pros: A fitting and heartfelt finale that gives the series a proper sendoff while leaving the door open for future adventures.
Sarah Myer delivers standout artwork, with expressive character work, exciting action sequences, and memorable villain designs.
A celebration of the 1987 TMNT legacy that combines the humor, heart, and colorful fun of the cartoon.
cons: The central rescue plot is fairly straightforward, relying on familiar tropes even if Burnham adds some nice character moments.
